title: The Last Ledger Revisited
premise: True-crime podcaster Coral Hartwell has spent years solving cold cases from the margins, never seeking credit. When a confession letter for the 1994 drowning of dockworker Elias Vann arrives postmarked the day after the sender's funeral, Coral is pulled into the orbit of Harrow Bay, a company town where the shipping dynasty that owned everything also owned every verdict. Following a ledger of bribes hidden in plain sight, Coral discovers the confessor, retired clerk Miriam Oduya, confessed to protect her son—and that the real killer still holds power over the town's courts and police. As witnesses die and Coral's own past in Harrow Bay surfaces, they must choose between publishing safely and testifying at personal cost; the story ends with Coral broadcasting the ledger, the dynasty's heir arrested, and Coral finally claiming a place—messy, public, and belonging—in the town they once fled.
about_author: Ivo Ashgrove is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing port-town records along the northern coast before turning to fiction. Their novels are known for procedural precision, morally tangled investigators, and small towns that keep their secrets in triplicate.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A week after wrapping their third solved case, Coral receives a handwritten confession to a thirty-year-old drowning, postmarked the day after the sender's funeral. The letter names names Coral has never published. Emotional beat: the thrill of a new case curdles into unease—someone knew how to reach them.

chapters.title: The Town That Kept Books
chapters.summary: Coral travels to Harrow Bay, a fog-bound port dominated by the Verrone shipping family. POV alternates between Coral's arrival and archival excerpts of the town's centennial booklet. Emotional beat: claustrophobic charm; everyone smiles like they're being recorded.

chapters.title: Elias Vann, 1961–1994
chapters.summary: Coral reconstructs the victim: a dockworker who fell from Pier Nine, ruled accidental. Interviews his estranged daughter, Tamsin, who remembers her father warning someone off the books. Emotional beat: grief as an inheritance; Tamsin's guarded hope.

chapters.title: Miriam Oduya's Quiet Room
chapters.summary: Coral tracks the letter to Miriam Oduya, a deceased court clerk, and interviews her neighbor, who recalls Miriam burning papers in her final months. Emotional beat: tenderness toward a dead woman Coral can never question.

chapters.title: Alibi, Thirty Years Cold
chapters.summary: The confession claims Miriam saw the killing but stayed silent. Coral cross-references her court docket entries against the official timeline and finds three records altered in her hand. Emotional beat: the vertigo of realizing the paper trail was curated.

chapters.title: The Heir Apparent
chapters.summary: POV shifts briefly to Julian Verrone, now the family patriarch and sitting county judge, hosting a charity regatta. He learns a podcaster is asking about Pier Nine. Emotional beat: polished menace; power exercised through hospitality.

chapters.title: What the Water Keeps
chapters.summary: Coral dives the pilings at Pier Nine with a salvage contact and finds a rusted strongbox wedged below the waterline. Emotional beat: physical dread and triumph—the first object the town couldn't rewrite.

chapters.title: Ledger of Small Sins
chapters.summary: Inside the box: a partial ledger of payments to police, coroner, and press, initials only. Coral matches initials to living people, including the current sheriff's father. Emotional beat: the sickening scale of ordinary corruption.

chapters.title: A Warning, Politely Worded
chapters.summary: Coral's hotel room is searched; their recording equipment returned slightly rearranged. Sheriff Dane Colm 'advises' them to leave town. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into defiance.

chapters.title: The Son Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Coral locates Miriam's son, Daniel Oduya, a withdrawn ferry mechanic. He admits his mother confessed to shield him—he was on the pier that night and saw nothing but ran. Emotional beat: shame passed down like a family trade.

chapters.title: Three Accidents, One Pattern
chapters.summary: Coral maps two other 'accidents' from the nineties onto the ledger's payment dates: a journalist and a union organizer. All three threatened the Verrone books. Emotional beat: pattern recognition as horror—the case was never singular.

chapters.title: Tamsin's Testimony
chapters.summary: Tamsin reveals her father kept a duplicate page sewn into a coat she still owns. The page names 'J.V.' beside a payment dated the night before the drowning. Emotional beat: vindication shadowed by terror of what naming him will cost.

chapters.title: The Archive Fire
chapters.summary: A fire guts the county records annex, destroying the original docket. Coral barely escapes while pulling Miriam's personal file. Emotional beat: rage; the enemy is erasing history faster than Coral can read it.

chapters.title: Invisible No More
chapters.summary: Julian Verrone invites Coral to dinner—a velvet threat wrapped in charm, offering funding and silence in one breath. Coral declines and records it. Emotional beat: Coral realizes invisibility, their old armor, is gone forever.

chapters.title: Daniel Breaks
chapters.summary: Daniel, pressured by anonymous calls, attempts to flee town but instead comes to Coral, surrendering a letter Miriam wrote naming the man she saw: not Julian, but his enforcer, Ray Cutler—still alive, still employed by the family. Emotional beat: relief complicated by a new target.

chapters.title: Ray Cutler's Version
chapters.summary: Coral confronts Cutler at a marina bar. He neither confirms nor denies, but lets slip that the drowning was meant as a warning that went wrong. Emotional beat: chilling banality; evil as routine maintenance.

chapters.title: The Deputy Who Kept Copies
chapters.summary: A retired deputy, one of the ledger's initials, approaches Coral offering the full ledger in exchange for immunity framing—an ethical trap. Coral must decide whether justice can be bought secondhand. Emotional beat: moral compromise pressing on the throat.

chapters.title: Deadline at the Regatta
chapters.summary: Cutler is found dead—genuine accident or cleanup?—and Julian announces he'll preside over a defamation suit against Coral's podcast. Time collapses; publication must happen before the injunction lands. Emotional beat: sprinting tension, allies assembling.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Coral publishes the full ledger, the altered dockets, and the dinner recording in a live episode from the Harrow Bay pier, with Tamsin and Daniel speaking on air. Emotional beat: catharsis; the town listening to its own name said aloud.

chapters.title: What the Judge Knew
chapters.summary: State investigators move in; Julian is suspended and charged with obstruction and conspiracy, though the drowning itself remains legally ambiguous—Miriam's word against a dead man's silence. Emotional beat: justice arriving imperfect, which is to say real.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Coral confronts the cost: sources burned, Daniel hospitalized after retaliation, their anonymity permanently forfeited. They visit Miriam's grave and read her the episode's download numbers. Emotional beat: mourning and accountability entwined.

chapters.title: Belonging
chapters.summary: Months later, Coral returns to open a small archive of the case in the rebuilt annex, co-run with Tamsin. The town that once erased its dead now keeps their records in daylight. Emotional beat: quiet resolution—Coral stops passing through and stays.
